canonicalExplanation.summary: Where `const` sits decides **what** is protected. Read declarations **right to left**. `const int *p` (same as `int const *p`) is "p is a pointer to const int": you **can't change the int through p**, but p can point elsewhere. `int *const p` is "p is a const pointer to int": p **can't be re-pointed**, but the int can be changed. `const int *const p` locks both. In function signatures, `const int *` promises the caller **"I'll only read your data"**, and the compiler enforces it. Give each parameter the **least** mutation right it needs.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner's `print_scores(int *scores, size_t n)` accidentally contains `scores[i] = 0;` left over from debugging, and it silently wipes the caller's data. A teammate says "just add const", and the learner writes `int *const scores`, which doesn't stop the bug. const int *p permits p to select another int but prevents modifying an int through p. In this lesson you'll design a pointer-based function signature with the least required mutation rights.

```predict
{"question": "With `const int *p = &a;`, which line is an error?", "options": ["p = &b;", "*p = 5;"], "answer": 1, "why": "The int is read-only through p; p itself can move."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **One-dimensional arrays**, **Parameters and return values**, **Addresses and dereference** and **Declarations, prototypes and definitions**.

sections.heading: The distinction: const on the data or on the pointer
sections.body:
```c
int a = 1, b = 2;

const int *p1 = &a;     /* pointer to const int. */
p1 = &b;                /* ok: the pointer can move. */
/* *p1 = 5;   error: can't modify through p1. */

int *const p2 = &a;     /* const pointer to int. */
*p2 = 5;                /* ok: a is now 5. */
/* p2 = &b;   error: p2 can't be re-pointed. */

const int *const p3 = &a;   /* neither can change. */

/* Least rights in signatures. */
void print_scores(const int *scores, size_t n);   /* reads only. */
void reset_scores(int *scores, size_t n);         /* writes, visibly. */
```

| Declaration (read right to left) | Change the int? | Re-point? |
|---|---|---|
| `const int *p`. | no. | yes. |
| `int *const p`. | yes. | no. |
| `const int *const p`. | no. | no. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Does const int *p make the int itself constant everywhere?", "answer": "No. It only restricts access through p. If a is a plain int, other code (or another pointer) can still change it. const on a pointer is a promise about this access path."}
```

sections.heading: Passing to const

examples.title: Read-only access, movable pointer
examples.situation: const int *p permits p to select another int but prevents modifying an int through p.
walkthrough: **const int *p permits p to select another int:** in print_scores, p can step through the array with p++.
**But prevents modifying an int through p:** the leftover `scores[i] = 0;` now fails to compile.
**Least rights:** the signature becomes print_scores(const int *scores, size_t n), and callers will know their data is safe.
examples.result: The debugging leftover is caught by the compiler instead of wiping data.

examples.title: The wrong const
examples.situation: The learner first wrote `int *const scores`, and `scores[i] = 0;` still compiled.
walkthrough: int *const makes the pointer fixed, not the ints.
The data the bug touched was still writable.
Move const to the left of the *: const int *scores.
examples.result: The right thing is protected: the caller's data.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: const int * and int * const mean the same thing because both contain the word const.
misconceptions.correction: const left of * protects the pointed-to data through that pointer; const right of * fixes the pointer itself. They protect different things.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The wrong const", why did the bad write still compile?

analogy.example: `const int *` is like **a museum visitor's pass**: you can walk to any exhibit (re-point) but can't touch them (modify). `int *const` is **a guard posted at one exhibit**: they can't move, but they can adjust that exhibit. `const int *const` is **a camera fixed on one exhibit**: no moving, no touching.
usefulFor: remembering visitor vs guard vs camera
limitations: Museum rules bind everyone; const binds only that pointer.
Adding a restriction (visitor pass) is always allowed.

farTransfer.prompt: Write signatures (and bodies) for: count_matches (reads an array), fill (writes an array), find_first (returns a pointer into a read-only array) and copy (reads one array, writes another). Give each parameter the least rights.

remediation.explanation: For each pointer parameter ask: **will this function modify what it points at?** If not, make it const int *. Then read the declaration right to left to check.

recap.summary: To design const-correct signatures, read declarations right to left, use const int * for data a function only reads, int *const when the pointer itself must not move, and give each parameter the least mutation rights it needs, remembering const restricts one access path, not the object everywhere.
